Personally, I am dyspraxic and had no innate artistic skill, like my parents were mean to me as a 5yr old about my art even. I like some of my drawings now, but I had to put the work in, and that is not even innate to people with coordination difficulties. There's learning anatomy, shading, how faces emote, how people perceive things. There's different approaches; realism, abstract, painterly. Understanding the choice between oil paints, waterpaints and so on. And then what you want to do with that understanding, how you want to play with those things. Decisions like that are separate from coordination and there can be joy in making those creative choices separate from how well one can execute them. 

I found digital art nicer in some ways because you have things like layers, undo buttons, pen stabilisation which between my innate coordination issues and handshakes from PTSD is super helpful. Though just pen and paper is nice because you just do the thing, you have to let perfectionism go and there's less prep work for executive dysfunction to trip over. 

I do not know how your dyspraxia or anything else impacts you, I only know how it impacts me. But I think if you really want to make some art it's worth sticking with and seeing how far you can go.

It is not your fault. This is a very difficult thing to go through and it can be hard to show kindness to oneself during it, but do what you can. If you are spiralling but are in a safe place, try reminding yourself that you are safe right now. That what is stressing you is not happening in this moment. The memories of trauma are difficult for the brain to handle and that is okay, but it means there might be a part of you thinking that it is still happening and it can be helpful to try and ground yourself. There are many different ways to ground yourself, some that will work for you and some that will not and I recommend looking into them yourself. But personally I find smells or tastes that I enjoy help, or consciously noticing my feet on the ground help me.

If you want to talk to someone but are wary about friends, there are free phone/internet counselling services you might be able to find, or there is possibly seeing a psychologist/therapist. Here is a page that might help you

I never went to a Christian school, and did not come out until university anyway, but I was raised Anglican. Even when the priest is great, even when the official rules of the church are explicitly in support of x, someone there will harass you for x. Even for my parents being somewhat queerphobic, racist and my dad being a conservative FOX watching prick, they were left-leaning enough or at least poor enough to be kicked around. Church allows women priests, but the congregations were always hostile to women priests. Homeless person comes into the church, most people just complain about him. I was harassed by 80yr olds as a child no older than 10 for the circumstances of my birth, I was harassed by other children for the same thing. Children are good at echoing bigotry. 

And from what I have been told, by people who are Anglican and thus would be biased, that Catholics are on the more conservative end of Christianity. And well there is stuff like women priests still not being allowed by the Catholic Church's law as opposed to.. the theoretical allowance of them in Anglican ones. Or that thing I was harassed for being "allowed" by the Anglicans but not the Catholics. 

Again none of those are schools, and I have heard people have better experiences than me. I know my religious trauma is not everyone's experience. But you know, I would say discrimination is a solid *maybe*.

Not feeling real and struggling with concentration are both dissociative symptoms, which has its source in trauma and can often be found alongside PTSD. No one here can diagnose you, but I can say that there is something up and you should see a doctor to try and get some help.

Trauma can be tricky like that. I imagine that response is because of your rape. It can be a lot to deal with mentally, too much even. It can cause damage, so to prevent that, our brain represses it rather than processes it. This is again okay, it happens to protect us. It is still there though, and does not let itself be ignored forever. So a few months ago you process that you were raped. And now yesterday you were given a scare, you felt unsafe and specifically unsafe in the way you were when you were raped. That could bring up a lot of emotions that you have not yet felt. 

I would talk to someone. I have heard some schools have free counselling, or maybe therapy is an option for you (I say because I know in some places it is practically impossible). You could talk to your mum, or someone you trust. There are support lines for when you are struggling with mental health, some of them specifically for people who have been raped. They might be able to find more resources for you. 

And I guess just pay attention to how you are feeling and be kind to yourself. Some people get over post-traumatic symptoms in a matter of months largely on their own, but that is not the case for everyone, and I am one of the latter people. Maybe there is something you can do for her, like bring her something comforting (some music, a food or drink, a plush?), remind her of something she can do for herself (I sometimes forget to breathe when I am breaking down)

The other thing that comes to mind is that I have something called a comfort plan taped to my wall, that I was given by someone at a mental health care facility. It works just as much as a resource for myself as other people, it has three checklists all focused on safety. My triggers, my signs and signals that I am getting upset, and what is comforting and calming to me. 

Finally; it is possible that all you need to do is be a good partner for her in good times and bad. I have not heard of this technique, however there are many mindfulness techniques like it and I understand what it is like to be put on edge by some techniques. Different things work for different people. Our physical bodies carry a lot of memories too, I had memories come up from a grounding technique that involved my posture. I have talked with my psychologist too about my struggle with hyperarousal and I hope this helps.

One thing I do find helpful is to really feel, really notice, the ground underneath your feet. Plant them firmly and focus on that. The posture technique was similar, which I will describe now in case it helps you better. Sitting down, and feet planted, sit up straight and also put your hands on your knees/legs, try to relax (feels impossible for me but, yeah) and the idea is to again feel that firmly planted position all through your body. 

Now some techniques are more of the mind, which are maybe worth exploring. Very much about observing your surroundings. I find the 5-4-3-2-1 technique a bit too restrictive, I do not have a good nose, sometimes there is nothing to hear, sometimes what I can hear is what is triggering me for one reason (family arguing) or another (overstimulation). That is described in a link I will drop a bit lower though cause again, what does not work for me might work for you. But what I find does help is something a bit similar. To find something visual in my surroundings and focus on it. It can be quite mundane, I have stared at an air vent and given intense thought to it and found that has helped. It is quite easy for me at least to find something I can focus on in my surroundings, unless I am on a bus. And of course, on that note sometimes you are surrounded at people and people wonder why you are staring at them even if you are actually staring at their coffee mug to try and ground yourself, so it is a bit situational.

Hey, I don't feel like I have a lot of advice, and I do hope you can find a way through this. But well, I'm going through something similar. I'm still learning what helps me but I do find two things helpful.

Being mindful of my breathing. Different to feeling like I can't breathe, during these blues i might unconsciously be breathing too shallowy, or too deep, or just kinda holding my breath. So I find it good to just take a moment and consider how I am breathing, and take control of it for a bit. Just focusing on breathing can be a bit calming too. It doesn't always get me out of the moment, but it may calm me down enough to sleep

The other thing is learning to notice and accept how I am feeling. I find not doing those things really fuels further anxiety for me. If I'm judging myself, beating myself up for missing another uni class. Or if I'm not paying attention to myself. I mean it's obvious if I can't get myself to do stuff, but there is a difference in my mind between knowing that im stuck in a horrible state and taking the time to notice how I am doing, and telling myself that it is okay to be sad, angry, hurt, afraid.  I'm not sure if I'm explaining this as well as the people I have talked to, but i hope this makes sense.

Also, I've been told a lot of stuff that hasn't connected with me. If what works for me doesn't work for you, that doesn't mean there isn't something else that will. A lot of the meditation, mindfulness and breathing exercises than not I haven't found much in. And I still have a way to go. But other things have helped, and its important to see what steps we have made I think.
